---
title: "8 Production and productivity of economic systems"
---

## 8.1 The production function {#sec-production-function}

The production function expresses a relationship between input and output: the former represents the factors used to produce (factors of production), the most important of which are labour $L$ and capital $K$; the latter the value of the goods and/or services produced (GDP or value added). The advent of technology and of new forms of production processes has in fact excluded other variables, such as land, from the econometric specification, and in other cases has included additional factors, such as the energy required by the process or the education and skills of the workforce. In any case, labour and capital are still the most relevant inputs and often the only ones considered in the statistical and econometric specification of the function, if only because of the difficulty of defining and measuring the other variables.

In a form such as

$$
Y=f(L,K)
\tag{8.1}
$$

output $Y$ is usually measured by value added (VA), especially in a macroeconomic approach. For consistency of sources and proper comparability of the data, $L$ is commonly measured by the number of full-time equivalent labour units (ULA), while $K$ is measured by gross private fixed capital, given the difficulty of subtracting depreciation (the value of capital consumption) without excessive arbitrariness.

Value added and labour units raise fewer estimation problems, while capital is generally computed indirectly, not without complications, by applying the perpetual inventory method to investment: an estimate of the capital stock at some date in the past is obtained, and investment is added while retirements are subtracted and depreciation is taken into account (at least for the net valuation); but even the valuation of retirements is not simple, being represented by mathematical forms based on somewhat arbitrary assumptions.

The difficulty of estimating private capital is quite evident from the ISTAT time series (among them, those valued at replacement cost are preferable); for the country as a whole, time series cover fewer than 30 years, while territorially disaggregated estimates and estimates for the most recent years are missing.

The problems increase if, following a more complex formulation, one decides to add an estimate of public capital, usually denoted by $G$ and corresponding in practice to public works. The working assumptions are even stronger in this case: is it right to assume that the value of an investment in a motorway lasts 80 years? How can a secondary road be distinguished from a main road? Should one not account for some wear (more in some places, less in others) of public works? And so on.

Function (8.1) does not satisfy part of the literature, which proposes adding an estimate of public capital $G$ and an estimate of the capabilities, skills and, in general, abilities of the workforce through a suitable measure of human capital $H$. The educational level of the employed can be a good proxy for $H$, on the assumption that higher levels of education (especially technical and scientific training) are strongly correlated with the ability to perform a given job.

The production function might therefore become

$$
Y=f(L,K,G,H)
\tag{8.2}
$$

The statistical limits in defining and measuring some of the inputs that characterise mathematical forms such as (8.2) go together with non-negligible difficulties in the correct economic interpretation of the estimated coefficients. In short, weighing the pros and cons, it is advisable to use the simpler and more easily interpretable traditional forms, in particular the Cobb-Douglas production function which, moreover, with slight adjustments allows technological change to be taken into account, a rather complex operation in more elaborate mathematical forms. Hence, despite the many criticisms raised, the Cobb-Douglas is still widely applied, mainly because its estimates are easier to interpret.

## 8.2 The Cobb-Douglas function and returns to scale {#sec-cobb-douglas}

In its basic formulation the Cobb-Douglas (CD) is

$$
Y=aL^{\alpha}K^{\beta}\varepsilon
\tag{8.3}
$$

It is therefore non-linear in the parameters and must be linearised by taking logarithms

$$
\log Y=\log a+\alpha \log L+\beta \log K+\mu
\tag{8.4}
$$

At this point OLS estimators can be used, provided, as usual, that the statistical conditions for a good regression estimate hold.

The CD is a homogeneous function of degree $\alpha +\beta$. In particular, if $\alpha +\beta =1$ we say there are constant returns to scale; that is, if inputs increase by a factor $k$, output increases proportionally by the same factor. If $\alpha +\beta <1$, there are decreasing returns to scale: if inputs increase by a scale factor $k$, output grows less than proportionally. Conversely, if $\alpha +\beta >1$, output grows more than proportionally to inputs. Clearly $\alpha +\beta =1$ is a desirable equilibrium condition, but there is generally no economic or statistical reason to assume that this constraint holds a priori.

We load the data in the file *funzprod.csv*, on output, labour and capital in the agricultural sector of Taiwan over 1958-1972, expressed in millions of local dollars at constant prices and in millions of working days. We estimate the Cobb-Douglas function linearised in logarithms

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
fp <- read.csv2("data/funzprod.csv")
attach(fp)
cd <- lm(log(Y)~log(L)+log(K))
round(summary(cd)$coeff,3)
```

### Python

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from scipy import stats

def coef(m):
    """Coefficient table, like summary(m)$coeff in R."""
    return m.summary2().tables[1].iloc[:, :4].round(3)

fp = pd.read_csv("data/funzprod.csv", sep=";", decimal=",")
cd = smf.ols("np.log(Y) ~ np.log(L) + np.log(K)", data=fp).fit()
print(coef(cd))
```

### SAS

```sas
data fp;
  infile "data/funzprod.csv" dlm=";" firstobs=2;
  input anni Y :commax12. L :commax12. K :commax12.;   /* the comma is the decimal separator */
  logY = log(Y); logL = log(L); logK = log(K);
run;
proc reg data=fp outest=stime_cd;
  cd: model logY = logL logK;
run;
quit;
```
:::

The estimated coefficient of the first regressor is 1.499, while that of the second is 0.490; their sum is well above one

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
summary(cd)$coeff[2]+summary(cd)$coeff[3]
detach(fp)
```

### Python

```{python}
print(cd.params.iloc[1] + cd.params.iloc[2])
```

### SAS

```sas
data _null_;
  set stime_cd;
  total = logL + logK;
  put total=;
run;
```
:::

so returns to scale are increasing.

Under the hypothesis that $\alpha +\beta =1$, then $\beta =1-\alpha$ and the functional specification becomes

$$
Y=aL^{\alpha}K^{1-\alpha}
\tag{8.5}
$$

Dividing both sides by $L$ we have

$$
Y/L=aL^{\alpha -1}K^{1-\alpha}=a(1/L^{1-\alpha})K^{1-\alpha}=a(K/L)^{\beta}
\tag{8.6}
$$

that is, the partial productivity of labour $Y/L$ is a function of capital intensity $K/L$ through a multiplicative form with exponent $\beta$.

The file *messico.csv* reports GDP and capital in millions of real pesos and employment in thousands for Mexico between 1955 and 1974. The Cobb-Douglas estimate is therefore

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
mex <- read.csv2("data/messico.csv")
attach(mex)
messico1 <- lm(log(Y)~log(L)+log(K))
round(summary(messico1)$coeff,3)
```

### Python

```{python}
mex = pd.read_csv("data/messico.csv", sep=";", decimal=",")
Y, L, K = mex["Y"].to_numpy(float), mex["L"].to_numpy(float), mex["K"].to_numpy(float)
messico1 = smf.ols("np.log(Y) ~ np.log(L) + np.log(K)", data=mex).fit()
print(coef(messico1))
```

### SAS

```sas
proc import datafile="data/messico.csv" out=mex dbms=dlm replace;
  delimiter=";"; getnames=yes;
run;
data mex;
  set mex;
  logY = log(Y); logL = log(L); logK = log(K);
  logYL = log(Y/L); logKL = log(K/L);
run;
proc reg data=mex outest=stime1;
  messico1: model logY = logL logK;
run;
quit;
```
:::

with apparently increasing returns to scale

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
rendim <- summary(messico1)$coeff[2]+summary(messico1)$coeff[3]
rendim
```

### Python

```{python}
rendim = messico1.params.iloc[1] + messico1.params.iloc[2]
print(rendim)
```

### SAS

```sas
data _null_;
  set stime1;
  rendim = logL + logK;
  put rendim=;
run;
```
:::

Of course the estimated returns might not be statistically different from 1. If so, the extended and the restricted models would not be sufficiently different. We can test this hypothesis with an $F$ statistic we already know

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
messico2 <- lm(log(Y/L)~log(K/L))
round(summary(messico2)$coeff,3)
ris <- sum(messico2$residuals^2)
uns <- sum(messico1$residuals^2)
Fr <- ((ris-uns)/1)/(uns/(20-3))
Fr
pf(Fr,1,17,lower.tail=FALSE)
```

### Python

```{python}
messico2 = smf.ols("np.log(Y/L) ~ np.log(K/L)", data=mex).fit()
print(coef(messico2))
ris = np.sum(messico2.resid ** 2)
uns = np.sum(messico1.resid ** 2)
Fr = ((ris - uns) / 1) / (uns / (20 - 3))
print(Fr, stats.f.sf(Fr, 1, 17))
```

### SAS

```sas
proc reg data=mex outest=stime2;
  messico2: model logYL = logKL;
run;
quit;
/* the same F test, directly on the unrestricted model */
proc reg data=mex;
  messico1: model logY = logL logK;
  returns: test logL + logK = 1;
run;
quit;
```
:::

The $F$ statistic suggests accepting, at the 95% level, the null hypothesis of constant returns to scale, i.e. $\alpha +\beta =1$. Moreover, since the estimated coefficient of the regressor in the restricted model is 1.015, a 1% increase in capital intensity leads to an increase of about 1% in labour productivity. This is certainly an anomalous result, since it gives $\beta$ values close to one and $\alpha$ values close to zero. In particular, the negative estimate of $\alpha$ is mainly due to a statistical anomaly for a coefficient here considered close to zero.

## 8.3 Elasticities, marginal productivities and Euler's theorem {#sec-elasticities}

Recalling that

$$
\partial Y/\partial L=a\alpha L^{\alpha -1}K^{1-\alpha}
\tag{8.7}
$$

and since the elasticity $e$ is the ratio of two relative changes, which in the case of labour are $\Delta Y/Y$ and $\Delta L/L$, we have

$$
e=(\Delta Y/Y)/(\Delta L/L)
\tag{8.8}
$$

and, in continuous terms,

$$
e=(\partial Y/\partial L)/(Y/L)=a\alpha L^{\alpha -1}K^{1-\alpha}/a(K/L)^{1-\alpha}=\alpha
\tag{8.9}
$$

so the elasticity of $Y$ with respect to $L$ (i.e. $e_{L}$) is exactly $\alpha$. Similarly, the elasticity of $Y$ with respect to capital $K$ ($e_{K}$) is $\beta =1-\alpha$. Therefore, if $L$ increases by $k\%$, $Y$ increases by $k\alpha \%$, and if $K$ increases by $k\%$, $Y$ increases by $k(1-\alpha )\%$.

Hence, if

$$
e_{L}=(\partial Y/\partial L)/(Y/L)=\alpha \qquad \text{and} \qquad e_{K}=(\partial Y/\partial K)/(Y/K)=\beta
\tag{8.10}
$$

then also

$$
\partial Y/\partial L=\alpha (Y/L) \qquad \text{and} \qquad \partial Y/\partial K=\beta (Y/K)=(1-\alpha )(Y/K)
\tag{8.11}
$$

Consequently, the marginal productivity of labour is $\alpha$-proportional to the average productivity of labour, while the marginal productivity of capital is $\beta$-proportional to the average productivity of capital.

Indeed, with the data for Mexico we obtain approximately (in the restricted model the estimated coefficient is $\beta$, hence $\alpha =1-\beta$)

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
beta <- summary(messico2)$coeff[2]
a <- exp(summary(messico2)$coeff[1])
round((a*(1-beta)*L^(-beta)*K^(beta) -Y/L*(1-beta)),1)
```

### Python

```{python}
beta = messico2.params.iloc[1]
a = np.exp(messico2.params.iloc[0])
print(np.round(a * (1 - beta) * L ** (-beta) * K ** beta - Y / L * (1 - beta), 1) + 0)
```

### SAS

```sas
data _null_;
  set stime2;
  call symputx("beta", logKL);
  call symputx("a", exp(Intercept));
run;
data marg;
  set mex;
  diff = round(&a*(1-&beta)*L**(-&beta)*K**(&beta) - Y/L*(1-&beta), 0.1);
run;
proc print data=marg noobs; var anni diff; run;
```
:::

while by Euler's theorem we can also write

$$
Y=(\partial Y/\partial L)L+(\partial Y/\partial K)K
\tag{8.12}
$$

since

$$
\begin{gathered}Y/Y=1=(\partial Y/\partial L)(L/Y)+(\partial Y/\partial K)(K/Y)= \\ \alpha (Y/L)(L/Y)+(1-\alpha )(Y/K)(K/Y)=\alpha +(1-\alpha )=1\end{gathered}
\tag{8.13}
$$

and, therefore, output $Y$ is entirely attributed to the two factors of production $L$ and $K$ according to their productivities. It is easy to obtain the corresponding decomposition and to check that it adds back up to output $Y$ with the data for Mexico

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
round((((1-beta)*Y/L)*L),0)
round(((beta*Y/K)*K),0)
round((((1-beta)*Y/L)*L),0)+round(((beta*Y/K)*K),0)-Y
```

### Python

```{python}
shareL = np.round((1 - beta) * Y / L * L)
shareK = np.round(beta * Y / K * K)
print(shareL.astype(int)); print(shareK.astype(int))
print((shareL + shareK - Y).astype(int))
```

### SAS

```sas
data euler;
  set mex;
  shareL = round(((1-&beta)*Y/L)*L, 1);
  shareK = round((&beta*Y/K)*K, 1);
  check = shareL + shareK - Y;
run;
proc print data=euler noobs; var anni shareL shareK check; run;
```
:::

Note the unusual negative value for the labour factor.

Following marginalist theory under perfect competition, the productivity of a factor must equal its relative price

$$
\partial Y/\partial L=P_{L}=\alpha (Y/L) \qquad \text{and} \qquad \partial Y/\partial K=P_{K}=(1-\alpha )(Y/K)
\tag{8.14}
$$

It follows that

$$
\begin{gathered}Y=P_{L}L+P_{K}K=\alpha (Y/L)L+(1-\alpha )(Y/K)K= \\ \alpha Y+(1-\alpha )Y=Y\end{gathered}
\tag{8.15}
$$

that is, $\alpha$ is also the share of $Y$ attributable to labour and $(1-\alpha)$ the share attributable to capital.

If $Y=aL^{\alpha}K^{\beta}$ with $\log Y=\log a+\alpha \log L+\beta \log K$, defining $\nabla Z=Z_{t}-Z_{t-1}$ for any variable $Z$ at each time $t$, it follows that

$$
\nabla \log Y=\alpha \nabla \log L+\beta \nabla \log K
\tag{8.16}
$$

Since $\nabla \log$ is the growth rate, we conclude that the growth rate of output $Y$ is approximately the weighted sum of the growth rates of the inputs labour $L$ and capital $K$. We obtain

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
dL <- diff(log(L))*(1-beta); dK <- diff(log(K))*beta
round(diff(log(Y))-dL-dK,1)
detach(mex)
```

### Python

```{python}
dL = np.diff(np.log(L)) * (1 - beta); dK = np.diff(np.log(K)) * beta
print(np.round(np.diff(np.log(Y)) - dL - dK, 1) + 0)
```

### SAS

```sas
data growth;
  set mex;
  dY = dif(log(Y)); dL = dif(log(L))*(1-&beta); dK = dif(log(K))*&beta;
  if _n_ > 1 then gap = round(dY - dL - dK, 0.1);
run;
proc print data=growth(firstobs=2) noobs; var anni gap; run;
```
:::

The implicit assumptions, legitimate for adjacent periods, are the stability of the coefficients $\alpha$ and $\beta$ and an unchanged technology, which become untenable over long periods.

Therefore, to account explicitly for the effect of technology, one can use Solow's well-known formulation, in which technical progress is computed as a residual. We can write (the usual conditions of neoclassical theory hold, with $\alpha +\beta =1$)

$$
Y=A(t)L^{\alpha}K^{\beta}
\tag{8.17}
$$

where $A(t)$ represents the effect of technical progress.

Hence $\log Y=\log A(t)+\alpha \log L+\beta \log K$ and, differencing over periods, $\nabla \log Y=\nabla \log A(t)+\alpha \nabla \log L+\beta \nabla \log K$, which gives the Solow residual

$$
\nabla \log A(t)=\nabla \log Y-(\alpha \nabla \log L+\beta \nabla \log K)
\tag{8.18}
$$

It is also interesting to note that $Y=A(t)L^{\alpha}K^{\beta}$ can be rewritten as

$$
A(t)=Y/L^{\alpha}K^{\beta}=TFP
\tag{8.19}
$$

In this formulation $A(t)$ is not linked to the Solow residual but to a measure of total factor productivity (TFP), since it is the ratio of output $Y$ to a combination of the two factors of production through a geometric mean with weights $\alpha$ and $\beta$. Thus an index of how TFP changes over time (or space) is simply a total productivity index, given by the ratio of two TFPs for different periods (or areas). In essence, this is a non-parametric method with strict assumptions: perfectly competitive markets, constant returns to scale, Hicks-neutral technical progress (i.e. technical progress changes the marginal productivity of the factors in the same proportion), and no adjustment costs (so firms always tend towards a long-run equilibrium).

## 8.4 Total factor productivity in Italy {#sec-tfp}

The file *prodita.csv* reports value added and net capital in millions of constant 2000 euro, and labour units in thousands, for Italy between 1980 and 2007, under the hypothesis (to be verified) that it is admissible to set $\alpha =0.2$ and $\beta =(1-\alpha )=0.8$. Total factor productivity with base year 2000 = 100 is easily obtained

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
prod <- read.csv2("data/prodita.csv")
attach(prod)
tfp <- VA00/((L^0.2)*(K00^0.8))
round((tfp/tfp[21]*100),2)
```

### Python

```{python}
prod = pd.read_csv("data/prodita.csv", sep=";", decimal=",")
VA00, L, K00 = prod["VA00"].to_numpy(), prod["L"].to_numpy(), prod["K00"].to_numpy()
tfp = VA00 / ((L ** 0.2) * (K00 ** 0.8))
print(np.round(tfp / tfp[20] * 100, 2))   # year 2000 is the 21st element
```

### SAS

```sas
data prod;
  infile "data/prodita.csv" dlm=";" firstobs=2;
  input anni VA00 :commax16. L :commax12. K00 :commax16.;   /* the comma is the decimal separator */
  tfp = VA00/((L**0.2)*(K00**0.8));
  if anni = 2000 then call symputx("tfp2000", tfp);
run;
data prod;
  set prod;
  tfp100 = round(tfp/&tfp2000*100, 0.01);
run;
proc print data=prod noobs; var anni tfp100; run;
```
:::

We observe small fluctuations between 1980 and 2007; indeed

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
round(tfp,4)
```

### Python

```{python}
print(np.round(tfp, 4))
```

### SAS

```sas
proc print data=prod noobs; var anni tfp; format tfp 8.4; run;
```
:::

Labour productivity (here in thousands of euro) shows a substantial increase, while capital productivity is broadly stable

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
round(VA00/L,2)
round(VA00/K00,4)
```

### Python

```{python}
print(np.round(VA00 / L, 2))
print(np.round(VA00 / K00, 4))
```

### SAS

```sas
data prod;
  set prod;
  prodL = round(VA00/L, 0.01);
  prodK = round(VA00/K00, 0.0001);
run;
proc print data=prod noobs; var anni prodL prodK; run;
```
:::

To explain the strong increase in labour productivity, from about 33 thousand euro in 1980 to about 46 thousand euro in 2007, let us decompose the ratio of value added to labour units into two specific components.

Since $Y/L=Y(1/L)$, it follows that $\log (Y/L)=\log Y-\log L$, i.e. the growth rate of productivity is (approximately) the growth rate of value added minus that of labour units

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
dYL <- diff(log(VA00/L))
dY <- diff(log(VA00))
dL <- diff(log(L))
round(dYL*100,2)
round(dY*100,2)
round(dL*100,2)
```

### Python

```{python}
dYL = np.diff(np.log(VA00 / L))
dY = np.diff(np.log(VA00))
dL = np.diff(np.log(L))
for v in (dYL, dY, dL):
    print(np.round(v * 100, 2))
```

### SAS

```sas
data rates;
  set prod;
  dYL = round(dif(log(VA00/L))*100, 0.01);
  dY  = round(dif(log(VA00))*100, 0.01);
  dL  = round(dif(log(L))*100, 0.01);
run;
proc print data=rates(firstobs=2) noobs; var anni dYL dY dL; run;
```
:::

In this case, which uses actual data for Italy, it is interesting to note that a 0.72% increase in labour productivity between 2006 and 2007 is explained by a 1.67% increase in value added and a 0.95% increase in labour units. By contrast, between 1980 and 1981 a 0.85% increase in labour productivity is almost entirely due to the increase in output of about 0.83%, the change in labour being almost nil (slightly negative, -0.01%).

## 8.5 Technical progress in the Cobb-Douglas {#sec-technical-progress}

The functional specification of the Cobb-Douglas can be enriched by an additional variable expressing technical progress acting over time; in this way one could capture improvements in input quality over time, such as a progressively better-qualified workforce or machinery able to produce faster and with less waste. In this case we could write

$$
Y=aL^{\alpha}K^{\beta}e^{ut}
\tag{8.20}
$$

Clearly, if $\alpha +\beta =1$ were imposed when it does not hold, the term $e^{ut}$ would also absorb the effects of returns to scale.

Estimating the model we obtain

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
summary(lm(log(VA00)~log(L)+log(K00)+I(c(1:28))))
```

### Python

```{python}
prod["t"] = np.arange(1, 29)
mod_t = smf.ols("np.log(VA00) ~ np.log(L) + np.log(K00) + t", data=prod).fit()
print(mod_t.summary())
```

### SAS

```sas
data prod;
  set prod;
  logVA = log(VA00); logL = log(L); logK = log(K00);
  t = _n_;
run;
proc reg data=prod;
  progress: model logVA = logL logK t;
run;
quit;
```
:::

Only capital appears significant, while the trend factor (which here represents the effect on output of technical progress as the mere passing of time) is not only non-significant but even has a slightly negative coefficient. Note that the intercept is also negative. We will not dwell on these anomalous results, since the discussion would move on to topics already covered in the previous chapters on the statistical analysis of linear models, the limits of functional-form specification and the problems of stationarity of the series.

Finally, note that in the Cobb-Douglas specification with technical progress, changes in labour quality can also be considered explicitly through a measure of hours worked. For example

$$
Y=aL^{\alpha}K^{\beta}h^{T}e^{ut}
\tag{8.21}
$$

where $h$ is the average number of hours worked per employee.

## 8.6 More general forms: CES, VES and translog {#sec-translog}

To conclude, it is worth mentioning production functions that are more general than the CD, but also less used in empirical analysis because they are harder to interpret and to estimate statistically. In particular, the Cobb-Douglas has a constant elasticity of substitution (between $L$ and $K$) equal to one; this assumption is not always admissible. There are more complex forms that remove some of these constraints, for example functions with a constant elasticity of substitution not necessarily equal to one, the so-called CES functions. VES functions, similarly, generalise to the case of a non-constant elasticity of substitution; among these forms the best known is the translog

$$
\begin{gathered}\log Y=b_{0}+b_{1}\log L+b_{2}\log K+b_{3}(\log L)^{2}+ \\ b_{4}(\log K)^{2}+b_{5}(\log L\log K)\end{gathered}
\tag{8.22}
$$

We obtain

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
trans <- lm(log(VA00)~log(L)+log(K00)+I(log(L)^2)+I(log(K00)^2)+I(log(L)*log(K00)))
summary(trans)
detach(prod)
```

### Python

```{python}
trans = smf.ols("np.log(VA00) ~ np.log(L) + np.log(K00) + I(np.log(L)**2)"
                " + I(np.log(K00)**2) + I(np.log(L)*np.log(K00))", data=prod).fit()
print(trans.summary())
```

### SAS

```sas
data prod;
  set prod;
  logL2 = logL**2; logK2 = logK**2; logLK = logL*logK;
run;
proc reg data=prod;
  translog: model logVA = logL logK logL2 logK2 logLK;
run;
quit;
```
:::

Here too there would be much to say about the correct specification of the model, but we leave the topic aside since it is not the subject of this section.
